lab_title: Shaping Molecules: Predicting 3D Geometry with VSEPR Theory
top_level_objectives: Explain the central principle of VSEPR theory — that electron domains around a central atom orient to minimize mutual repulsion.
Translate a Lewis structure into a count of bonding and lone-pair electron domains around the central atom.
Identify the five fundamental electron-domain geometries (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral) and the bond angles associated with each.
Predict how lone pairs convert an electron-domain geometry into a distinct molecular geometry (bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, square pyramidal).
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, accounting for bond-angle deviations such as 104.5° in water versus 109.5° in methane.
Match VSEPR predictions to the observed structures of real molecules including water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4.

scenes.scene_name: The Core Idea: Electron Pairs Repel
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the foundational principle of VSEPR — that regions of electron density around a central atom push apart to maximize separation — before any specific geometry is named.
key_visuals: A single central atom rendered in the center of the AR space with glowing electron-domain clouds attached to it.
Animated repulsion arrows showing two and three domains sliding apart until they reach maximum mutual angle.
A simple on-screen meter labeled 'Total Repulsion' that drops as domains spread out.
student_actions: Grab and drag two electron-domain clouds on a central atom and observe the repulsion meter rise as they are forced close together.
Release the domains and watch them settle into the lowest-repulsion arrangement (180° apart).
Add a third domain and confirm the system relaxes into a flat 120° arrangement.

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis Structure to Domain Count
scenes.brief_purpose: Bridge prior knowledge of 2D Lewis structures to the 3D domain-counting step that drives every VSEPR prediction.
key_visuals: A flat Lewis structure of a sample molecule (e.g., CH4 or H2O) floating beside the 3D central atom.
Highlight overlays that tag each bond as a 'bonding domain' and each lone pair as a 'lone-pair domain'.
A running tally counter showing the number of bonding domains, lone-pair domains, and total electron domains.
student_actions: Tap each bond and lone pair in the Lewis structure to classify it as bonding or lone-pair.
Confirm the total electron-domain count populated on the central atom.
Submit the domain count to unlock the corresponding electron-domain geometry.

scenes.brief_purpose: Build a systematic mental library of the five parent geometries and their idealized bond angles by manipulating domain number directly.
key_visuals: The central atom cycling through 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 bonding domains with shapes snapping into linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements.
Floating angle labels (180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°/120°, 90°) appearing on each geometry.
A reference shelf where each completed geometry is stored as a labeled mini-model.
student_actions: Use a slider or +/- control to set the number of bonding domains from two to six.
Rotate each resulting geometry in 3D to inspect the spatial arrangement and read the bond angles.
Place each of the five completed parent geometries onto the reference shelf to confirm mastery.

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate that molecular geometry is defined by atom positions only, so swapping bonding domains for lone pairs produces new shapes from the same parent geometry.
key_visuals: A tetrahedral central atom whose bonding domains are converted one at a time into lone pairs, morphing into trigonal pyramidal then bent shapes.
A trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral atom transforming into seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, and square pyramidal as lone pairs are added.
Color-coding that distinguishes invisible lone-pair domains from visible bonded atoms in the named molecular shape.
student_actions: Toggle individual bonding domains into lone pairs on a chosen parent geometry.
Observe and name the resulting molecular geometry as the atoms rearrange.
Match each derived shape (bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square planar, square pyramidal) to its correct name in a labeling task.

scenes.scene_name: Why Lone Pairs Bend the Angles
scenes.brief_purpose: Explain the subtle bond-angle deviations from ideal values by showing that lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
key_visuals: Side-by-side methane and water central atoms with a live bond-angle readout.
An enlarged, more diffuse lone-pair cloud on the water oxygen visibly pressing the bonding pairs closer together.
A dynamic angle gauge animating from the idealized 109.5° down to the observed 104.5° as the lone-pair repulsion is applied.
student_actions: Compare the measured H–C–H angle in methane (109.5°) with the H–O–H angle in water (104.5°).
Increase the simulated lone-pair size and watch the bonding angle compress further.
Answer a short prompt ranking lone-pair/lone-pair, lone-pair/bonding, and bonding/bonding repulsion strengths.

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students apply the full VSEPR workflow independently to predict the geometry of an assigned molecule before any answer is revealed.
key_visuals: A molecule card (e.g., NH3, PF5, or XeF4) presented with its formula and a blank prediction panel.
An empty central-atom workspace where the student assembles domains.
A prediction submission panel with fields for electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
student_actions: Build the electron-domain arrangement for the assigned molecule by adding the correct bonding and lone-pair domains.
Select the predicted electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry from menus.
Submit the prediction to lock it in before validation.

scenes.scene_name: VSEPR vs. Reality: The Verification Gallery
scenes.brief_purpose: Confirm and consolidate learning by overlaying student predictions against the experimentally observed structures of benchmark molecules.
key_visuals: A gallery of real molecules — water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, XeF4 — each shown as an accurate 3D structure with measured bond angles.
A side-by-side overlay of the student's predicted shape ghosted onto the observed structure to highlight matches.
A summary scoreboard listing each molecule with its electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and bond angle.
student_actions: Overlay each predicted geometry onto the corresponding real molecule to verify the match.
Inspect the observed bond angles and note where lone pairs caused deviations from ideal values.
Complete a final summary table linking every benchmark molecule to its VSEPR-predicted shape and observed angles.
